title: Why your GPS needs Einstein
summary: GPS satellite clocks are built deliberately wrong so relativity makes them right.

title: Why honey never spoils
summary: Honey outlasts empires because it is a sealed desert too dry, too acidic, and too antiseptic for microbes to survive.

title: Why the microwave doesn't heat by resonance
summary: A microwave doesn't resonate water molecules; it twists them billions of times a second and the internal friction is the heat.

title: Why a bicycle stays up
summary: The gyroscope explanation for bicycle stability is wrong, and the real answer is one condition that several different mechanisms can satisfy.

title: The machine that seems to break physics
summary: A heat pump gives out three or four times the energy it uses because it moves heat instead of making it, and your refrigerator is the same machine pointed the other way.

title: How a tree beats the best pump on Earth
summary: Suction cannot lift water past ten meters, yet a redwood raises it a hundred, using stretched water under negative pressure pulled by evaporating leaves.

title: Half of you was made in a factory
summary: About half the nitrogen atoms in your body came out of an industrial reactor, because life cannot break the bond that locks nitrogen in the air.

title: The metal that was worth more than gold
summary: Aluminum is the most common metal in the crust, but it stayed invisible for all of human history because its grip on oxygen could only be broken by electricity.

title: Why ice is slippery
summary: The pressure melting story you were taught is wrong; ice is slippery because its top few molecular layers are already liquid before you touch them.

title: Why the sun is a terrible furnace
summary: The core of the sun makes less heat per cubic meter than your own body, and that feebleness is exactly why life had time to happen.

title: The invention is in the corners
summary: Shipping got cheap not because ships got faster but because a standardized steel box cut the cost of touching cargo by ninety seven percent.

title: Why glass is transparent
summary: Glass lets light through not because it has gaps, but because its electrons cannot absorb the energy visible light carries.

title: Why a haircut keeps getting expensive
summary: Services like teaching, nursing and live music get costlier every decade not because they got worse, but because everyone else got more productive.

title: Why your rice cooker has no timer
summary: A cheap rice cooker has no thermometer and no timer, yet it never overcooks rice, and the reason is a magnet tuned to give up three degrees above boiling.

title: The spring made of chaos
summary: A rubber band pulls back not because its bonds are stretched, but because tangled is overwhelmingly more likely than straight.

title: The traffic jam with nothing at the front
summary: Most traffic jams have no cause at all: they are waves built by ordinary careful drivers, and they roll backwards at about twelve miles an hour everywhere on Earth.

title: Stale bread is not dry bread
summary: Bread goes stale because its starch quietly recrystallizes, not because it loses water, which is why the fridge is the worst place for a loaf and a hot oven genuinely undoes it.

title: You breathe your fat away
summary: Most of the fat you lose leaves your body as carbon dioxide through your lungs, because atoms have to go somewhere.

title: The radioactive speck in your ceiling
summary: The common smoke detector holds a sliver of a man made element and never actually sees smoke, which explains why it can sleep through the fires that kill people.

title: The blue light wearing a costume
summary: There is no such thing as a white LED, and the blue one underneath it took thirty years because it only works by being badly made.

title: The little hole in the airplane window
summary: That tiny hole in the cabin window deliberately hands the entire pressure load to one pane, and the window's rounded shape was paid for in the nineteen fifties.

title: Why the night carries sound
summary: Sound does not just spread and fade, it steers: cold air near the ground at night bends distant sound back down to you, and the same physics once hid an entire battle from an army four miles away.

title: The bass note that isn't there
summary: The lowest note in a voice or a song is often not in the air at all; your brain rebuilds it from the spacing of the harmonics, which is why phone calls and coin sized speakers work.

title: The brakes that turn on when everything breaks
summary: Air pressure does not apply a train or truck brake, it holds the brake off, so the moment the system fails the brakes slam on by themselves.

title: Why a sailboat beats the wind
summary: A sail is a wing, a keel is a wing, and a boat gets squeezed forward between two fluids.

title: The sand you cannot build with
summary: Deserts are full of sand that is useless for concrete, because wind polishes every grain into a sphere and cement needs corners to grip.

title: The flywheel the size of a continent
summary: The power grid stores almost no energy, so the frequency in your wall is a live readout of whether the whole continent is making more power than it is using.

title: The bridge that taught a crowd to walk in step
summary: How London's Millennium Bridge and the people on it accidentally built a machine for amplifying a wobble, and why the same math runs fireflies and heartbeats.

title: The Moon is stealing the Earth's spin
summary: Why tides come twice a day, and how the friction they cause is pushing the Moon away and quietly making our days longer.

title: The digit that shows up too often
summary: In real world data the leading digit is a one about thirty percent of the time, because the world multiplies instead of adding, and auditors use that to spot invented numbers.

title: The lightning goes up
summary: The bright flash in a lightning strike travels from the ground into the cloud, and the sky and the earth build the channel together.

title: The lock picks itself
summary: A pin tumbler lock has one hundred thousand combinations on paper, but manufacturing tolerances make its pins give way one at a time, turning the secret into five easy questions.
